message.content: {"name":"end_turn","arguments":{"public_message":"Not hoteling. That just dumps houses for a Park Place build. Housing stays locked.","private_thought":"Status quo is correct. Cash $536 + 12 pink houses ($600) + pink mortgages ($220) = $1356 max, so PP 3h ($1100) or even 4h ($1300) is survivable only if I don't spend. BW 4h ($1700) still kills me. Do not hotel/sell (frees houses; p1 can mortgage KY+Atlantic and buy the 1 bank house onto PP). Do not unmortgage PRR/TN (-EV, no sets). Do not trade cash or TN (completes p4 oranges) or fund p1. p1 on Vermont has ~39% to hit a pink next (rolls 4/6/7); if they pay $750-900 they must strip dark-blue houses, then I build before p4. Keep GOOJF for a jail sit before dark blues. End turn."}}
message.reasoning:
I am reviewing the current Monopoly game state to determine my next move.

I have $536 and a pink monopoly with four houses on each property. I hold one Get Out of Jail Free card. The bank has one house and twelve hotels remaining. Player one is nearly broke with only $14 and heavily mortgaged holdings.

Player three is bankrupt. Player four has $1436 and owns light blues at four houses, plus railroads and greens. I am deciding between trading, unmortgaging, building, selling, or ending my turn. The priority is locking in my pink monopoly with four houses each. Hotel or sell decisions are avoided to preserve the last house in the bank.

Building a hotel would return four houses to the bank. That would free up the last house and let player one build on Park Place.

Player one cannot afford a house right now. Player four could hotel their light blues later, but the rent increase is small and the houses would be wasted.

Unmortgaging the Pennsylvania Railroad would cost $220 in interest. That is too expensive to justify right now.

Unmortgaging Tennessee Avenue would cost $99 and leave only $217. That is not worth the risk of landing on player one's dark blue properties or player four's light blue monopoly.

I am now evaluating trade offers with player one and player four.

Player one is currently on Vermont Avenue. Player four is on New York Avenue. The pink monopoly yields $750 to $900 in rent per visit. That would bankrupt player one immediately. Their only assets are the dark blue properties with three and four houses.

Player one could sell all seven dark blue houses for $700 and mortgage Park Place and Boardwalk for another $375. That would cover the $900 rent on Virginia Avenue.

I rejected trading Tennessee Avenue to player four. That would complete their orange monopoly and give them a dangerous set of houses they could build on.

Player four could complete a green monopoly by acquiring Pacific Avenue from player one. That would be dangerous, so I should not help that trade. I considered buying Pacific myself to block it, but receiving a mortgaged property in a trade requires paying 10% interest immediately.

Player four already owns a fully built light blue monopoly. Their only remaining green properties are mortgaged, and the bank holds just one house. That makes a green monopoly impossible to build right now. Blocking Pacific Avenue is therefore less urgent while the housing lock remains tight. Player four might still hotel their light blues later to free houses and attempt a green upgrade.

I must prevent player four from hoteling any light blue property. That would return four houses to the bank and break the housing lock, letting them build greens or player one build on Park Place. I cannot force player one to sell their dark blue houses.

Player four is unlikely to trade away their built light blue monopoly. I am on Tennessee Avenue, a mortgaged property that collects no rent. After resolving my landing, I will end my turn.

Player one cannot build yellows because Marvin Avenue is mortgaged, and they lack the $154 needed to unmortgage it. Their only viable threat remains the dark blue properties. Park Place needs one more house to reach four, but player one cannot afford the $200 upgrade.

I am now considering a trade with player four to acquire their mortgaged orange properties. That would give me a full orange monopoly and eliminate their threat. I rejected offering cash to player one because it would fund their Park Place house upgrade.

A full orange monopoly would require unmortgaging three properties for $308. The bank holds only one house, so building would be impossible. Receiving mortgaged properties in a trade also requires paying 10% interest immediately.

Player four likely will not trade their mortgaged orange properties for cash or a railroad. They know that completing my orange monopoly would be lethal once houses are available. I am weighing whether to offer cash plus the Pennsylvania Railroad for both St James Place and New York Avenue.

I will end my turn. Trading for one orange property is useless without the other two. I am liquidating my pink houses for $600, giving me about $1136 total cash and mortgaged assets. That should survive a dark blue hit.

Fully liquidating all houses leaves $1136, which barely covers a three-house Park Place hit of $1100. That would leave me with only $36 and no houses. I must avoid landing on dark blue properties entirely. Using my Get Out of Jail Free card to sit in jail is the correct strategy when approaching that side of the board.

I am on Tennessee Avenue. The next rolls will move me toward Free Parking, reds, yellows, and eventually dark blues. I cannot choose to go to jail on purpose. I should keep my Get Out of Jail Free card for when I actually need to leave jail.

I will not propose a trade. No offer is clearly profitable and acceptable to the other players.

I will keep my public message brief and consistent with earlier warnings. I am watching player four's turn order, since building is a post-turn action that could let them immediately rebuild returned houses on another monopoly.

Player four has no other buildable monopoly. Hoteling their light blues would return twelve houses to the bank, but player one cannot afford a Park Place house upgrade with only fourteen dollars. Player one could mortgage Kentucky, Atlantic, or Ventnor to raise cash, yet that would leave those properties mortgaged.

Player one could mortgage Kentucky, Atlantic, and Ventnor for $384. That would fund a Park Place house and possibly let them build yellows. Hoteling light blues would return four houses to the bank. Player one could then upgrade Park Place to four houses for $1300 rent. I will publicly warn player four against hoteling. I already said this on turn 115.

Building a hotel on the pink monopoly would free four houses but only raise rent by two hundred dollars. That is too small a gain to justify the cost. Selling houses would also weaken my rent and help player one or player four.

Unmortgaging the Pennsylvania Railroad would cost $220 for only $25 in rent. That is a terrible return. Unmortgaging Tennessee Avenue would also be unwise. Player four wants to win and likely needs either pink immunity or a complete green or orange monopoly.

Player one might trade Pacific Avenue for cash, but that property is mortgaged and operationally useless to them right now. Player four would not accept a deal that gives them nothing critical in exchange for their orange properties.

I calculated that buying Pacific Avenue for cash would cost roughly ninety-five dollars once interest is paid. That would leave me with only about four hundred forty-one dollars, which is still short of the one thousand one hundred dollar rent on Park Place after full liquidation. The trade would therefore make that dark blue threat unavoidable.

I must keep at least $1100 in liquidatable assets. Selling all houses yields only about $600, leaving a $36 surplus. Boardwalk would cost $1700, which is $564 short of survival. I am checking whether mortgaging the pink properties after selling houses could bridge that gap.

Mortgaging the pink properties adds roughly two hundred twenty dollars. Combined with house sales, total liquidation reaches about one thousand three hundred fifty-six dollars. That covers a three-house Park Place hit and leaves a two hundred fifty-six dollar surplus. Boardwalk remains unreachable by three hundred forty-four dollars.

I could spend up to about two hundred dollars and still survive a three-house Park Place hit, but that would leave me mortgaged and without houses. That would make me vulnerable to player four's light blue properties and any future builds. I must avoid spending cash unless the trade is worth more than the survival margin.

Player one is circling near Vermont, a light blue property owned by player four. I will keep my housing lock intact and avoid spending cash or trading away houses. I am considering a brief public message to reinforce that stance and remind player one of the danger from my pink monopoly.

I will keep my public message short and blunt. I may bluff that I am comfortable with the pink threat to avoid revealing weakness. Player one is at Vermont, which is two spaces from Connecticut and far from St Charles Place.

Player one's next roll will likely land on St Charles Place, States Avenue, or Virginia Avenue. Those three pink properties are all mortgaged and worth nothing to player one right now. That means they have a high chance of hitting my pink monopoly again.

Player one has only fourteen dollars cash. Selling all houses would raise seventy dollars, yet that is still short of the seven hundred fifty or nine hundred dollar pink rent. Unmortgaged dark blue properties could be mortgaged after houses are removed, but that would leave player one with no houses and no cash.

Player one could survive a nine hundred dollar pink rent by mortgaging dark blue properties after selling all houses. That would leave them with no houses on the dark blues. Player four could then reclaim those seven houses and rebuild on the light blues.

Player four cannot build on the light blues even with the returned houses. Hoteling consumes the existing four houses and returns them to the bank, but player four still lacks a second monopoly. The returned houses would only add to the bank's supply without enabling new construction.

Player one would have no cash to rebuild immediately if they mortgaged dark blue properties. I could upgrade my pink monopoly to hotels with the returned houses. Player one would lose their threat and pay rent, but player four could also grab those houses and hotel their light blues.

Player one is at the head of the turn order. They will likely land on a pink property next and pay rent. Player four follows immediately after them, so any returned houses would be available for player four to claim.

Player one's turn immediately precedes mine, so any houses they sell to pay rent would be available for me to build on during my own turn. Hoteling the pink monopoly would raise rent to nine hundred fifty dollars on St Charles and States, and eleven hundred dollars on Virginia. Hotel construction returns four houses to the bank before placing the hotel.

Hoteling all three pink properties would return twelve houses to the bank. I have no other monopolies to rebuild, so those houses would simply flood the supply for player one or player four. That makes hoteling the pink monopoly a net loss.

Only player one can currently use a bank house productively. He needs one more house on Park Place to reach four, raising rent from $1100 to $1300. Player four has no unbuilt monopolies to rebuild. Hoteling my pink monopoly would free houses that player one could then purchase.

Player one cannot afford the fourth Park Place house right now, so the housing lock is currently inactive. It remains a critical safeguard if he later acquires cash from GO or by mortgaging Kentucky, Atlantic, or Ventnor.

Player one could mortgage Kentucky and Atlantic for two hundred fifty-four dollars. That would cover the two hundred dollar fourth Park Place house. He has not built it yet. Perhaps he does not realize the bank holds a house. Or he is saving cash. Or his turn already passed.

I cannot remove the single house in the bank without building it myself. Hoteling my pink monopoly would not consume that house, since hotel construction replaces four existing houses rather than drawing from the bank supply. That house remains a latent threat if player one later mortgages dark blue properties and buys the fourth Park Place house.

I cannot consume the single house in the bank, so I will not hotel or sell. Player one may build the fourth Park Place house on his next turn and raise rent to $1300.

Liquidating everything would leave only fifty-six dollars, so I will not reduce cash. I will end my turn and warn player one that I am not freeing houses and that he is one roll from the pink monopoly.
